name: Crestfall Ordnance SCN-1 "Switchback"
description:
The Switchback is a single-handed, dual-feed compact scattergun built around a patented Rotary Breech Selector (RBS) mechanism that reads neural interface signals to swap active ammunition types between shots. The core innovation — dismissed as a gimmick until it showed up in every major contract dispute in GLMZ Districts 7 and 12 — is a 35mm motorized disc housed in the receiver that physically rotates one of two parallel feed channels into alignment with the barrel in 38 milliseconds, faster than the trigger-to-ignition mechanical lag in any production pistol.

The weapon has two completely independent loading systems that never mix. Port Alpha (right flank, red LED) feeds a 3-round polymer tube magazine loaded with 2.5-inch compact 00 buckshot shells. Port Beta (left flank, blue LED) feeds a rear-stacked 2-round steel magazine loaded with 12-gauge sabot slugs. Both feed channels run as isolated rails through the receiver until they hit the RBS disc, where only one is ever live. The disc is held in position by a spring-detent and only moves on an active motor command — meaning a dead battery or severed wire leaves the weapon locked to whatever was last selected, which is why every SCN-1 ships with the manual override lever.

The neural interface integration is intentionally low-bandwidth. The Switchback does not require premium BCI hardware. It pairs with any Tier-1 motor cortex interface via a passive grip sensor array embedded in the handle — eight copper contact rings under the polymer overmold that read skin conductance and micro-tension differentials in the palm and fingers. The onboard Ballistic Intent Module (BIM) chip, a 4mm silicon wafer soldered to the grip frame, runs a trained classifier against this signal stream. The classifier was calibrated on 12,000 hours of shooter data: when a wielder unconsciously shifts to a precision grip — the subtle forward press of the index finger, the slight rotation of the wrist inward toward the target — the BIM interprets this as slug intent and fires the RBS to Port Beta. When the grip is loose and lateral, indicating a sweeping or close-quarters threat, it locks to Port Alpha for buck. Neither mode requires a conscious thought. After roughly four hours of use, the BIM self-calibrates to the individual operator's grip patterns and achieves 97.3% selection accuracy under field conditions.

The conscious override is a micro-flex gesture: tightening the extensor carpi radialis muscle of the gun hand — the forearm tendon that lifts the back of the hand — while maintaining firing grip. The gesture is invisible externally but consistent enough across human anatomy that the BIM reads it reliably within 12ms. A single flex switches mode; holding the flex for 400ms locks the selection until released. Operators without neural interfaces use the physical thumb lever above the trigger guard — push forward for slug, pull back for buck, spring-returns to center to display current state.

The single-handed operation requires solving a hard physics problem: a standard 12-gauge compact shell generates roughly 12 foot-pounds of recoil, enough to hyperextend an unprepared wrist and flag the muzzle 60 degrees off target. Crestfall's solution is a two-part system. The grip backstrap houses a 14mm hydraulic kick buffer — a piston that compresses 8mm rearward under recoil, stretching the impulse peak from 8ms to 120ms and cutting perceived kick by roughly 40%. The barrel terminates in a three-port Crestfall muzzle compensator that routes expanding gas upward through ported cuts, counteracting muzzle flip. The net result is a weapon that most augmented operators can fire accurately in rapid succession from one hand, and that baseline-human operators can fire without injury at the cost of wrist fatigue past round four or five. Wrist reinforcement cyberware or a tactical shooting glove eliminates this limitation entirely.

Cycling is manual — a 40mm travel slide with a ambidextrous thumb-tab at the rear of the receiver. After firing, the slide racks back to eject the spent shell from the 4-o'clock ejection port (downward-right, away from the eye line), then forward to strip the next round from whichever feed channel the RBS is currently aligned to. The ejector is a dual-geometry extractor that handles both the polymer buckshot hull and the brass-capped slug casing without modification. Advanced operators use a wrist-snap cycle technique — a sharp downward flick of the gun hand leverages inertia to cycle the slide without thumb contact — unreliable under adrenaline but useful when the trigger hand is otherwise occupied.

Reloading each port is independent. Port Alpha reloads from the right side: rounds are thumb-pressed into the tube magazine through a loading gate behind the ejection port, each clicking past a spring-loaded retaining lip. Three rounds load in approximately six seconds with practice. Port Beta reloads from the rear: a hinged steel baseplate at the back of the receiver drops on a finger-tab press, and two slug cartridges are dropped in nose-forward against a spring follower, then the plate is snapped shut. Both operations are possible one-handed, though only the Port Alpha tube load is fast enough to do in a running firefight.

The receiver rear face carries a three-state LED strip: red for buck active, blue for slug active, yellow-flicker during RBS rotation (the 38ms window when neither round is chamberable), and dark when the neural interface is not linked. A secondary indicator — a 2mm steel pin on the left grip panel — rises flush when buck is selected and protrudes when slug is active, giving a tactile read without breaking eye contact.
manufacturer: Crestfall Ordnance (Tier-3 independent, GLMZ District 4 fabrication license)
tier_availability: Tier 2–3 (street modified); original production Tier 4 (military surplus, increasingly rare)
legality: Illegal in all corporate-administered zones without special operations licensing. Common in inter-district gray markets. Confiscated units are frequently re-issued to enforcement contractors with BIM chips reflashed to corponation-specific neural signatures — effectively making the weapon inoperable without the correct employer's interface key.
base_technologies: Tier-1 neural interface (BCI motor cortex passthrough)
Ballistic Intent Module (BIM) — grip-mounted neural classifier
Hydraulic Kick Buffer (HKB) — backstrap piston recoil system
specifications: Caliber: 12-gauge compact (2.5-inch chamber). Barrel length: 7.5 inches (ported, partial rifling at final 3 inches for slug stabilization). Overall length: 11.2 inches (no stock). Weight unloaded: 1.4 kg. Capacity: 3+2 (3x buck Port Alpha, 2x slug Port Beta). RBS rotation speed: 38ms. HKB stroke: 8mm. BIM calibration period: ~4 hours field use for full individual accuracy. Neural interface requirement: BCI Tier-1 motor cortex passthrough, any manufacturer. Battery: 72-hour continuous standby on integrated microcell (grip base, user-replaceable). Manual override: thumb lever, ambidextrous.
tactical_use: The Switchback defines a category of engagement where a single operator needs to shift between area-denial and precision fire without drawing a second weapon. In doorway entry, buck clears a room and slug takes a head shot through the gap before the body has finished falling — both from the same one-handed weapon while the other hand holds a frame or restrains a target. Freelance contractors use it as a backup primary rather than a sidearm: shorter than a carbine, more decisive than a pistol, with the neural-select closing the gap between 'I need range' and 'I need spread' to less than a thought. The BIM accuracy limitation — the 2.7% misfire rate in the wrong mode under extreme stress — is considered acceptable compared to the time cost of manually switching weapons. Known weakness: the RBS disc is a precision mechanical component. Sand, slag dust, and blood in the receiver will jam rotation. Urban and indoor operators report no issues; wasteland users often disable the RBS entirely and hard-lock to one port.
cultural_context: The Switchback appeared in GLMZ approximately eleven years ago as a Crestfall Ordnance limited production run marketed to corporate security contracts. It flopped commercially — the BIM technology was too new, the price point too high, and the neural interface requirement excluded a large share of the private security market at the time. The remaining inventory bled into the gray market after Crestfall's District 4 facility was seized in a corponation territorial acquisition. With no active manufacturer and perhaps 1,400 units in circulation, the Switchback has become a status weapon among freelance operators who understand its mechanics. Finding one in working order implies the owner is technical, deliberate, and almost certainly not using it for the first time. The name 'Splicer' entered street use because early adopters described the neural-select as 'splicing your intent into the gun.' It has since taken on broader connotations: a Splicer is someone who adapts, who shifts modes, who never commits to one approach until the last moment. Carrying a Switchback is a statement about how you solve problems.
story_hooks: A functional SCN-1 surfaces at a dead drop intended for someone else — the BIM chip inside is still calibrated to a neural signature that matches a person who, according to every official record, died three years ago.

A contractor's Switchback begins selecting the wrong mode under stress — always switching to slug at close range, always to buck at distance. The BIM chip is factory-sealed and non-modifiable. Someone updated its classifier remotely, and the only way to do that is through the neural interface it's paired to.

Crestfall Ordnance didn't disappear. The District 4 facility seizure was staged. Someone needs the original BIM training dataset — 12,000 hours of shooter neural data — and the only person who knows where it went is the engineer who walked out the day before the 'acquisition.'
ammunition_type: Specialty load compatibility: incendiary buck (Port Alpha), armor-piercing slug (Port Beta) — requires manual BIM mode lock to prevent neural misfire
